# Hexagon bins {#sec-hex-bins} ::: {.callout-tip appearance='simple' icon=false} ***This graph is largely complete and just needs final proof reading.*** ::: :::: {.callout-note collapse="false" icon=false}
::: {.cell layout-align="right"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](hex_bins_files/figure-html/full_code_display-1.png){fig-align='right' width=60% height=60%} ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #02577A;"} **Requirements:** ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; color: #282b2d;"} **✅ two numeric (continuous) variable** ::: :::: ## Description Hexagon bins (or hex-bins) are very similar to 2-D histograms, but instead of dividing the graph area into a grid, it's divided into hexagons. The number of points inside each hexagon determines its color. ## Set up ::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"} **PACKAGES:** ::: Install packages. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} install.packages(c("hexbin", "colorspace")) library(colorspace) library(ggplot2) library(dplyr) # for tibble() and data manipulation ``` ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"} **DATA:** ::: Surge launched in 1997 as Coca-Cola's answer to Mountain Dew, and it was marketed straight at teenagers who played a lot of video games. We'll simulate 3,000 students with four variables: - `school` and `console`: drawn with `sample()` (Nintendo 64 or PlayStation) - `cans_per_week`: how many cans of Surge each student drinks in a week. Most students drink a few and a few drink a lot, so we draw these from a right skewed gamma distribution with `rgamma()`. College students average 6 cans, high school students 4, and middle school students 2 - `game_hours`: hours of video games per week, which go up 1.5 hours for every can of Surge, plus 2 hours for PlayStation owners, plus noise from `rnorm()` Setting the seed with `set.seed()` means you'll get the same 3,000 students every time you run the code below. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} set.seed(1996) surge_teens <- tibble( teen_id = 1:3000, school = sample(c("Middle school", "High school", "College"), size = 3000, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.3, 0.4, 0.3)), console = sample(c("Nintendo 64", "PlayStation"), size = 3000, replace = TRUE)) |> mutate( avg_cans = c(`Middle school` = 2, `High school` = 4, College = 6)[school], cans_per_week = round(rgamma(n(), shape = 2, rate = 2 / avg_cans), 1), game_hours = round(pmax(0, 3 + 1.5 * cans_per_week + if_else(console == "PlayStation", 2, 0) + rnorm(n(), mean = 0, sd = 3)), 1)) |> select(-avg_cans) glimpse(surge_teens) #> Rows: 3,000 #> Columns: 5 #> $ teen_id 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9,… #> $ school "Middle school", "High sch… #> $ console "Nintendo 64", "PlayStatio… #> $ cans_per_week 1.8, 0.9, 1.1, 0.8, 5.2, 6… #> $ game_hours 7.1, 6.1, 2.8, 8.2, 10.5, … ``` ::: ::: ## Distribution Every hexagon in a hex bin plot is a count, and the size of the hexagons controls how big those counts are. Big hexagons hold lots of students each, so their colors are steady but blurry. Small hexagons show more detail, but each one holds only a few students, so their colors are noisy. Below we'll move from the counts, to a picture, to the formula. ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **COUNT IT:** ::: Start with the first five students. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} head(surge_teens, 5) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ::: `layer_data()` returns the data behind a `ggplot2` layer, including the `count` in every hexagon. Below we compare the counts for 15 bins and 40 bins. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} hex_counts <- function(bins) { hex_plot <- ggplot(surge_teens, aes(x = cans_per_week, y = game_hours)) + geom_hex(bins = bins) layer_data(hex_plot) |> summarise(bins = bins, hexagons = n(), max_count = max(count), median_count = median(count), under_5 = mean(count < 5)) } hex_compare <- bind_rows(hex_counts(15), hex_counts(40)) hex_compare ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ::: With 15 bins, 88 hexagons hold the 3,000 students, and the median hexagon holds 7.5 of them. With 40 bins, there are 364 hexagons, the median hexagon holds only 3 students, and 59% of the hexagons hold fewer than five. ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **DRAW IT:** ::: The two graphs below draw the same students with 15 and 40 bins. Both show the same rising cloud (more Surge, more video games) that's crowded in the lower left. The 15 bin version is smooth. The 40 bin version shows more of the shape, but it speckles at the edges, where neighboring hexagons with counts of 1, 2, and 3 sit side by side. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell layout-ncol="2"} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} ggplot(surge_teens, aes(x = cans_per_week, y = game_hours)) + geom_hex(bins = 15) + labs(title = "15 bins", x = "Cans per week", y = "Hours of games") + theme(legend.position = "bottom") ggplot(surge_teens, aes(x = cans_per_week, y = game_hours)) + geom_hex(bins = 40) + labs(title = "40 bins", x = "Cans per week", y = "Hours of games") + theme(legend.position = "bottom") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](hex_bins_files/figure-html/draw_hex-1.png){width=576} ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](hex_bins_files/figure-html/draw_hex-2.png){width=576} ::: ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **NAME IT:** ::: The cans come from a [gamma distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamma_distribution) (right skewed), and the hours come from a normal distribution centered on a straight line: $$ \text{cans} \sim \text{Gamma}\left(k = 2, \; \theta = \frac{\text{avg cans}}{2}\right), \quad \text{hours} \mid \text{cans} \sim \text{Normal}(3 + 1.5 \times \text{cans} + 2 \times \text{PlayStation}, \; 3) $$ The skew in the cans is why the hexagons pile up in the lower left and thin out to the right. The count in each hexagon is approximately [Poisson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poisson_distribution) with a mean of $\lambda = 3000 \times p$, where $p$ is the chance a student lands in that hexagon. A Poisson count wobbles by about $\sqrt{\lambda}$, so its *relative* noise is $\sqrt{\lambda} / \lambda = 1 / \sqrt{\lambda}$. A hexagon expecting 100 students is off by about 10%, but a hexagon expecting 4 students is off by about 50%. Smaller hexagons mean smaller $\lambda$, and that's where the speckles come from. Try changing `size = 3000` to `size = 30000` and the 40 bin graph smooths out. ## Grammar ::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"} **CODE:** ::: - Create labels with `labs()` - Initialize the graph with `ggplot()` and provide `data` - Map `cans_per_week` to the `x` and `game_hours` to the `y` - Add the `geom_hex()` layer ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} labs_hex <- labs( title = "Surge soda and video games", subtitle = "Cans per week vs. hours of video games per week", caption = "Simulated data", x = "Cans of Surge per week", y = "Gaming hours per week") # graph ggp2_hex <- ggplot(data = surge_teens, aes(x = cans_per_week, y = game_hours)) + geom_hex() ggp2_hex + labs_hex ``` ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"} **GRAPH:** ::: ::: {.cell layout-nrow="1"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](hex_bins_files/figure-html/create_graph_hex-1.png){width=100% height=100%} ::: ::: ## More info ### Bins Below we change the `bins` to `20` and `15` and save these layers as `ggp2_hex_b20` and `ggp2_hex_b15`. *Decreasing* the number of `bins` *increases* the size of the hexagons. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} ggp2_hex_b20 <- ggplot(data = surge_teens, aes(x = cans_per_week, y = game_hours)) + geom_hex(bins = 20) ggp2_hex_b20 + labs_hex ggp2_hex_b15 <- ggplot(data = surge_teens, aes(x = cans_per_week, y = game_hours)) + geom_hex(bins = 15) ggp2_hex_b15 + labs_hex ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](hex_bins_files/figure-html/code_graph_hex_bins-1.png){width=576} ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](hex_bins_files/figure-html/code_graph_hex_bins-2.png){width=576} ::: ::: ::: ### Scale - We can adjust the color scale using `scale_color_discrete_sequential()` from the `colorspace` package and setting `aesthetics` to `"fill"`. - If the hexagons overlap, we can use the `alpha` to make them slightly transparent. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} labs_hex2 <- labs( title = "Surge soda and video games", caption = "Simulated data", x = "Cans of Surge per week", y = "Gaming hours per week", fill = "Console") ggplot(data = surge_teens, aes(x = cans_per_week, y = game_hours)) + geom_hex(aes(fill = console), bins = 15, alpha = 3/4) + scale_color_discrete_sequential( aesthetics = "fill", rev = FALSE, palette = "Viridis") + labs_hex2 ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](hex_bins_files/figure-html/code_graph_hex_scale-1.png){width=576} ::: ::: ::: Get a full list of available color palettes using `hcl_palettes(type = "sequential")` ### Options - `binwidth` allows us to manually adjust the size of the hexagons. - `linewidth` is also helpful when using `alpha` for overlapping values. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} labs_hex3 <- labs( title = "Surge soda and video games", caption = "Simulated data", x = "Cans of Surge per week", y = "Gaming hours per week", fill = "School") ggplot(data = surge_teens, aes(x = cans_per_week, y = game_hours, fill = school)) + geom_hex(binwidth = c(1.5, 3), linewidth = 0.5, alpha = 3/4, color = "#000000") + scale_color_discrete_sequential( aesthetics = "fill", palette = "Dark Mint") + labs_hex3 ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](hex_bins_files/figure-html/code_graph_hex_options-1.png){width=576} ::: ::: ::: Bins can be set with `bins` (a single number) or `binwidth` (a numeric vector of `c(x, y)`)
